binders: q is the solution field being averaged; the inherited one-dimensional presentation permits q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝᵐ, with spatial argument x and temporal argument t [printed p. 1, paragraph containing (1.1)].
A grid cell is a spatial piece of the domain; the definition applies to each such cell [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “over each grid cell”].

Time is held fixed when forming a spatial cell integral; this is inherited from q(x,t) integrated against dx in (1.10), rather than explicitly rebound in the defining sentence [printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2].
hypotheses: The domain is broken into grid cells in the finite volume description [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “we break the domain into grid cells”].

The defining sentence presupposes that the relevant cell integral and division by cell volume are meaningful; it supplies no explicit integrability, measurability, or nonzero-volume hypotheses [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, cell-average defining clause].
conclusions: For each grid cell, its cell average of q is the integral of q over that cell divided by the volume of the same cell [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “this integral divided by the volume of the cell”].

Finite volume methods approximate these cell integrals or cell averages, and the approximate values are modified at each time step using fluxes through cell edges [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph].

Numerical flux functions approximate the correct fluxes using the approximate cell averages as the available data [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “based on the approximate cell averages, the only data available”].
definitions_and_conventions: In analyst-introduced notation C for a cell, the definition reads average_C q(t) = (∫_C q(x,t) dx) / volume(C); the source gives this definition in prose rather than introducing C or this displayed formula [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, defining clause; printed p. 4, (1.10)].

Volume denotes spatial cell volume; in the supplied one-dimensional context, the referenced integral is against dx over an interval [printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “volume of the cell”].

For vector-valued q, the integral and its scalar normalization represent averages of the conserved-density components; this interpretation follows from the component-density description and the vector-valued declaration of q [printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10); printed p. 1, paragraph containing (1.1)].

The exact cell average is the quantity defined by the integral quotient; the numerical method uses approximate cell averages [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, “approximate” and “approximate cell averages”].
implicit_context: The selected claim is a definition within a description of finite volume methods, rather than a numbered theorem with an explicit quantified hypothesis list [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph].

Conservation laws supply the physical interpretation of the cell integral as a total conserved amount and of boundary fluxes as its mechanism of change [printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, (1.10) and following paragraph].

Discontinuous solutions are part of the intended setting; classical differentiability of q is not a stated prerequisite for the cell-average definition [printed p. 5, continuation of Section 1.1.2 and opening of Section 1.2].

The constant-coefficient linear system on printed page 1 is introduced as a simplest case; the subsequent context also includes nonlinear conservation laws, so linearity and a fixed matrix A are not inherited requirements of the cell-average definition [printed p. 1, paragraph containing (1.1); printed p. 4, opening paragraph; printed p. 5, Section 1.2].

details: The numerator integrates q over the entire cell and the denominator is that same cell's volume [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, defining clause].

The referenced source context uses spatial dx integration, and does not introduce an arbitrary measure parameter or weighted averaging convention [printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2, defining clause].
The averaged field can depend on time, while the averaging region is spatial [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.1); printed p. 4, (1.10)].

The unknown can have m conserved-density components; the selected passage does not restrict its definition to scalar q [printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1); printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10)].
Cell averages provide the data from which numerical fluxes are computed and cell values updated [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph].

The neighboring-cell indices i−1 and i occur in the later Riemann-problem application, rather than as required indices in the definition itself [printed p. 5, Section 1.2.1, paragraph following (1.11)].

Preserve spatial cell integration at a given time; the cited integral form is ∫ q(x,t) dx [printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2].

Do not attribute an arbitrary-measure generalization, a weighted average, or a convention for zero-volume cells to this passage; none is specified in its definition or its cited integral form [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, defining clause; printed p. 4, (1.10)].

Do not make smoothness or constant-coefficient linearity a source-stated requirement of this definition; its enclosing discussion treats discontinuities and conservation laws more broadly [printed pp. 4–5, Sections 1.1.1–1.2].

contract_plain_english: The selected passage defines the cell average of a solution field as its integral over a spatial grid cell divided by that cell's volume. Finite volume methods approximate these averages and update the approximate values using boundary fluxes computed from the available approximate averages [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph]. The inherited context uses spatial dx integration at fixed time and permits vector-valued conserved densities and discontinuous solutions [printed p. 1, paragraph containing (1.1); printed p. 4, (1.10) and following paragraph; printed p. 5, continuation of Section 1.1.2]. The passage does not specify an arbitrary measure, analytic admissibility conditions, or behavior for zero-volume cells [printed p. 5, Section 1.2, defining clause].
